passages.happening:
The chapter goes back a month, to ‘the day Moses finished setting up the tabernacle’ (verse 1).

The twelve tribal leaders bring a gift: ‘six covered carts and twelve oxen’ (verse 3). God tells Moses, “Accept these gifts from them, that they may be used in the work of the Tent of Meeting” (verse 5). Moses gives two carts to the Gershonites and four to the Merarites. “But he did not give any to the Kohathites, since they were to carry on their shoulders the holy objects for which they were responsible” (verse 9).

Then the leaders come with offerings for the dedication of the altar, and God says, “Each day one leader is to present his offering for the dedication of the altar” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Exodus dates the setting up of the tabernacle to the first day of the first month of the second year (Exodus 40:17). That is a month before the census that opens this book. The story steps back in time because these gifts complete what chapters 1 to 6 began. The tribes have been counted and placed. The Levites have their loads. Now the tribes themselves give: the means to move the tent, and the gifts for its altar.

The carts are practical. The Gershonites carried the curtains and coverings, so they receive two carts. The Merarites carried the heavy frames, posts and bases, so they receive four. The Kohathites receive none. The ark, the table and the lampstand were to ride on men's shoulders, as chapter 4 laid down.

The leaders are the same twelve who helped with the census. Nobody commanded this gift. They brought it, and God told Moses to accept it. In a book that will soon be full of complaint, the first thing the leaders of Israel do is give.
passages.later:
Generations later David moved the ark on a new cart, and Uzzah died when he reached out to steady it (2 Samuel 6:3-7). David came to see that the ark should have been carried on the shoulders of Levites, as this law required (1 Chronicles 15:13-15).

The Hebrew word for an offering in this chapter is qorban, something brought near. It appears in the Gospels as Corban, when Jesus rebukes people who used such vows to avoid supporting their parents (Mark 7:11).
passages.asks: The leaders gave what the work needed, carts and oxen, and gave more to those with the heavier load. Ask what practical thing someone near you needs in order to carry what they have been given. And ask whether your giving follows need, or follows who will notice.

passages.happening:
“On the first day Nahshon son of Amminadab from the tribe of Judah drew near with his offering” (verse 12).

He brings a silver platter and a silver bowl, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil, and a gold dish filled with incense (verses 13-14). He brings a bull, a ram and a lamb for a burnt offering, a goat for a sin offering, and for a peace offering ‘two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old’ (verse 17).

On each of the next eleven days another leader comes, in the order in which the tribes camp and march. Each brings exactly the same gift, and each is written out in full.
passages.hearers:
With 89 verses, this is the longest chapter in the five books of Moses. Most of its length is one paragraph of six verses repeated twelve times, with only the day, the name and the tribe changed.

A modern writer would have given the paragraph once and added that the others did the same. The Bible does not, and many readers find this the hardest chapter in the book to get through. The repetition is the point.

Each tribe's gift is recorded in full. No tribe's offering is passed over as a copy of another's. None is larger than the rest. Judah, the biggest tribe, gives what Manasseh, the smallest, gives. Each leader ‘drew near’ in his own name, on his own day. Jewish interpreters have long seen in this an honor paid to each leader one by one.

The chapter reads like a record kept in an archive. Temples across the ancient world kept exact lists of gifts received, with weights and numbers. A silver platter of 130 shekels weighed perhaps three pounds.

The gifts cover every kind of sacrifice Israel offered. The burnt offering, burned whole, spoke of giving everything to God. The sin offering dealt with wrong and uncleanness. The peace offerings, the largest part by far, were shared meals eaten before God. To bring all of these at once was to open every part of Israel's worship.

The repetition also slows the reader to the pace of the event. This was twelve days of worship, one tribe at a time.
passages.later:
When Solomon dedicated the temple, the gifts were of the same kinds on a far larger scale (1 Kings 8:63).

The Hebrew word for ‘dedication’ here is chanukkah. It later gave its name to the Jewish festival of Hanukkah, which remembers the rededication of the temple in 164 BC after King Antiochus IV had defiled it. John's Gospel shows Jesus in the temple at that festival: “At that time the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem. It was winter” (John 10:22).

Hebrews sets sacrifices that are repeated beside the one offering of Christ: “But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible repeat the same list of gifts twelve times?

The question is fair, and several answers work together. The chapter keeps the style of an ancient record, in which each giver's gift was entered separately and in full. The repetition also says something. By giving each tribe the same space and the same words, the text shows that no tribe's gift is worth less than another's. Some Jewish interpreters went further and found a separate meaning in each tribe's identical gift, drawn from that tribe's history, though that goes beyond what the text itself claims. And the length slows the reader down before the single short verse at the end, in which God speaks.

A reader who finds the chapter slow has not read it wrongly. It is slow on purpose.
passages.asks: God had each gift written out in full, though all twelve were the same. Ask whether you believe that what you bring to God is noticed when it is no different from what a hundred others bring. And ask whose faithful, ordinary giving you have stopped seeing because it never changes.

passages.t: A voice from above the ark
passages.happening:
The gifts are added up: twelve silver platters, twelve silver bowls, twelve gold dishes (verse 84), and the animals for each kind of offering (verses 87-88).

Then the chapter ends with one verse of a different kind. “When Moses entered the Tent of Meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from between the two cherubim above the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony. Thus the LORD spoke to him” (verse 89).
passages.hearers:
After twelve days of giving, the chapter reaches its goal, and it is not a total. It is a voice.

The tabernacle was built so that God could live among his people and speak with them. He had promised Moses at Sinai that he would meet him above the cover of the ark. Now the promise is kept. Moses goes in, and God speaks.

The place is named with care. The ark was the gold-covered chest in the innermost room. Its lid, with a winged figure called a cherub at each end, is the mercy seat. The Hebrew word, kapporet, is related to the verb for making atonement, and it was there that blood was sprinkled once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The place where sin was dealt with is the place from which God spoke.

All the silver and gold and all the animals led to this. The gifts did not buy the voice. But the whole ordered life of the camp existed so that Israel could live within hearing of God.
passages.later:
God had promised this meeting when he first described the ark: “And I will meet with you there above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are over the ark of the Testimony” (Exodus 25:22).

The old Greek translation called the mercy seat hilasterion. Paul uses that word of Christ: “God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood” (Romans 3:25). And Hebrews says that God, who spoke in many ways in the past, ‘in these last days’ has ‘spoken to us by His Son’ (Hebrews 1:2).
passages.asks: The long chapter of giving ends with God speaking. Ask whether your worship has a place in it for listening, or whether it is all bringing and doing. And ask when you last opened the Bible expecting to be spoken to.
